sections.history: Tiruperumpuliyur, a village of the Kaveri delta a short distance from Thiruvaiyaru, is the Perumpuliyur of the Tevaram. The child-saint Sambandar sang a decad of verses to the Lord here, and so the temple is counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The name means the great tiger-town, and it belongs to the family of Puliyur shrines linked with the sage Vyaghrapada; temple lists place it among the Nava Puliyur, the nine Puliyur temples worshipped by Vyaghrapada and Patanjali. One local account holds that a brick shrine stood here before the seventh century and that the temple was afterwards rebuilt under the Cholas and again in Vijayanagara times. The village has kept its name for well over a thousand years.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, whose carvings have come down remarkably well preserved. The presiding lingam is held to be self-manifested, and the Lord is worshipped here as Vyakrapureeswarar, the Lord of the tiger-town. The goddess Soundara Nayaki, the beautiful lady, has her own east-facing shrine, where she is shown standing and blesses devotees in that posture. The Navagraha shrine is unusual: the nine planets are set facing the Sun at the centre, rather than turned in varied directions as in most temples. The sacred tree is the sarakondrai, the golden shower tree, and the holy water is that of the Kaveri.
sections.legends: The legend of Perumpuliyur is that of the sage Vyaghrapada, known in Tamil as Pulikkal Munivar, the sage with the tiger's feet. He learned of the glory of Nataraja of Thillai from his father, the sage Madhyandina, and made his way to Chidambaram to worship the Lord every day. The flowers for that worship had to be gathered from high branches before dawn, in the dark, and before the bees could touch them. Moved by his devotion, Shiva gave him the feet of a tiger, to climb trees with ease, and the eyes of a tiger, to see each flower clearly in the night. The shrines where he worshipped came to be called Puliyur, and Perumpuliyur is held among them. Together with Patanjali he is remembered as a witness of the Lord's cosmic dance.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed here as at every Shiva temple, and the Tamil-month festivals of the Kaveri delta are kept in the traditional manner. Devotees also remember the sage Vyaghrapada on days of special worship. Specific festival dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally before travelling.
sections.experience: Tiruperumpuliyur lies in the middle of green farmland, and the visit has the quiet of a village temple. Enter beneath the three-tiered gateway, pause at its well-kept carvings, and come to the sanctum of Vyakrapureeswarar before turning to Soundara Nayaki in her standing form. Do not miss the Navagraha shrine, where every planet turns toward the Sun. Devotees who love the story of Vyaghrapada often add this shrine to a pilgrimage that includes Chidambaram and the other Puliyur temples, and it pairs naturally with the Tevaram shrines around Thiruvaiyaru.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the village of Perumpuliyur, roughly 4 to 5 km from Thiruvaiyaru in Thanjavur district, among farmland; the postal address is Thillaisthanam post, via Thiruvaiyaru. Thanjavur is the nearest large town and railhead, and Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport. Local buses and autorickshaws from Thiruvaiyaru reach the village; a short taxi or auto ride is the easiest way to combine it with neighbouring Tevaram temples.
